utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. Our apologies for the delayed start. There were other matters to deal with. Before the next witness is being called in, I would, on behalf of the Chamber, like to put some comments related to yesterday's hearing on the record. The Chamber would like to make one final remark on the discussion that occurred at the end of last night's session. The Chamber is concerned about the position of the OTP. At page 26, line 18, of the transcript of yesterday, the Prosecution advised that, and I quote: "It is absolutely essential that the witness be able to leave tonight." The Chamber was guided by this during the session. Later, after the departure of the witness, the OTP told us and the Defence that the witness would be available today for further cross-examination. This is a serious contradiction. It must be borne in mind that the Chamber relies on information provided by the Prosecution regarding the availability of witnesses. Furthermore, the Chamber would like to stress that in accordance with Article 20 of the Statute, this trial must be expeditious and also fair with full respect for the rights of the accused and due regard for the protection of witnesses. The Chamber will do its utmost to ensure this, and the parties should also take this into account during examination of witnesses throughout the proceedings. The Chamber can't accept the position of the Prosecutor that the accused has to show of proof what he needs to ask the witness about, and this is taken from the record of yesterday: "... and of course the Judges, absolutely ..." We don't understand quite well what Mr. McCloskey was referring to yesterday. But on the record we have a clear message received. And therefore a last comment: The Chamber doesn't accept the attitude in which the Prosecutor yesterday was addressing the Chamber after the remark of Judge Mindua. Although Mr. McCloskey offered his apologies, the Chamber is concerned about this situation. We have to consider which measures have to be taken to make sure that this will not happen again. I hope that it's a clear message toward the Prosecution. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't want to discuss this matter today.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. President. I did want to place on the record, as you can see, Mr. McCloskey is not here today and so he is not obviously in a position to address the Trial Chamber. I did have an opportunity to speak with him yesterday, and he does and I think he has expressed his regret in the manner in which he addressed the Trial Chamber and in particular His Honourable Judge Mindua pursuant to those comments. He couldn't be here today because of a planned mission that was scheduled well in advance of the proceedings yesterday and obviously today, and I do - and I will abide by your instruction not to address the issue further - but I do want to briefly stress that under no circumstances would the Prosecution suggest to the Trial Chamber a course of action to take with respect to a witness as it concerns the fairness of the proceedings. That is inconsistent with the rights of the accused and also that invades the prerogative of the Trial Chamber to determine the appropriate course of action in these proceedings. I don't believe that Mr. McCloskey intended to suggest that to the Trial Chamber, and I don't think that any of the prior conduct on behalf of the Prosecution was directed to that end. So I just wanted to make that clear, and I'll leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua -- Judge Nyambe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think we can appreciate your comments, Mr. Vanderpuye, and your intervention, but in view of the fact that you were not present in court when this took place, I hardly believe you are in -- I don't think you are in a position to read the mind of Mr. McCloskey to tell us as to what he meant and what he did not mean. We observed his conduct in court yesterday. So we appreciate your intervention, as indeed we would expect from a team spirit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed this is the position of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I did -- if I didn't mention before, I did have an opportunity to discuss the proceedings with Mr. McCloskey after the conclusion of proceedings and I of course have read the transcript with respect to them and that's essentially the basis of my understanding of what happened. Obviously I'm not sitting on the Bench and I wasn't in court, so I don't know what your impressions were with respect to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, we should stop the discussion here. We don't want to lose court time. And the next witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Ibrahimefendic. Welcome to the Tribunal. Please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down and make yourself comfortable. First I would like to express my apologies that we had a delayed start. We were occupied by another matter. Ms. Hasan has questions for you during the examination-in-chief by the Prosecution. Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, and everyone else in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam Witness. Before I ask you my questions, could you please --

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Would you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I am Teufika Ibrahimefendic. I'm a psychotherapist from the centre for therapy and rehabilitation called Vive Zene from Tuzla. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Ms. Ibrahimefendic, have you recently had the opportunity to listen to your testimony from the Krstic case?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I listened to the entire testimony from 2002 the day before yesterday, this is, from the Krstic case.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: From 2000.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Was the evidence that you gave in the Krstic case true and accurate to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: This testimony was from ten years ago. It reflected the situation as it was at the time. It reflected the state of the traumatised persons at that time, and it reflected on their suffering and what I was doing during those years with them and what I managed to say in court about my work and about my experiences on that matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So in that context and given your knowledge and experiences at that time, were the answers that you gave true and accurate?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Of course they were true and accurate. But if we observe the traumatic process over the past ten years, you can add to the state the suffering and the symptoms that were evident at the time, you can add a large number of facts, you can describe their situation right now, the state of suffering right now, their individual needs, their individual suffering. That's on the one hand. On the other hand, you could also describe the social dimension of the trauma or the context in which they live, actually in which all of us are living, including myself, over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll be asking you some questions about that in just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: At this stage, Mr. President, if I can offer into evidence the transcript of Ms. Ibrahimefendic from -- of her testimony in the Krstic case, and that's 65 ter 1574, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit P1817. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And with your leave, Mr. President, if I may now read a summary of that testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. Please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Ms. Teufika Ibrahimefendic is a Bosnian Muslim born in 1948. She is a psychotherapist who has undergone medical and social work training. Educated in psychology and pedagogy at the University of Sarajevo, Ms. Ibrahimefendic went on to study war trauma and the psychosocial counselling of traumatised women and children. After working as a pediatric nurse and a psychiatric social worker at the clinical centre at the hospital in Tuzla, Ms. Ibrahimefendic assumed the position of the co-ordinator of Vive Zene, a multidisciplinary organisation for the treatment of victims of war trauma.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please slow down a bit while reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: In addition to co-ordinating the Vive Zene programme, Ms. Ibrahimefendic treated women and children who were victims of the 1995 events in Potocari and the separation of the women and children from the men and boys. The women she treated exhibited an exceptionally high level of trauma. At the time of her testimony in the Krstic trial in 2000, Ms. Ibrahimefendic reported that the women and children of Srebrenica were still suffering from the trauma which manifested itself in vivid memories, nightmares, fear, irritability, nervousness, aggressiveness, loss of concentration, avoidance, and in some cases, depression, apathy, passivity, as well as grief, loss of motivation, and the will to live. Having treated other victims of trauma, Ms. Ibrahimefendic explained that the trauma suffered by the Srebrenica women was unique. The Srebrenica syndrome, as their trauma is described, is a consequence of the disappearance of their male family members, including their fathers, son, brothers, husbands, and uncles. Not knowing the truth of what happened to these men and their search for an explanation has been exhausting and discouraging for these women, who also carry with them a profound sense of guilt for the fate of these men. The children of Srebrenica, having witnessed the separation of their brothers and fathers, and having lived the adverse conditions in Potocari, also exhibited a high level of trauma. In addition to the trauma-induced symptoms experienced by these children, Ms. Ibrahimefendic observed that the absence of male role models in their lives stripped them of a sense of identity and impacted their enjoyment of life. The Srebrenica events left a lasting impact on the social lives of the surviving women and children. Ms. Ibrahimefendic gave evidence about the difficulties the women and children have encountered in re-establishing both familial and community relationships. The guilt the women of Srebrenica feel prevents them from declaring their missing husbands dead; a declaration that is a prerequisite for getting remarried. The difficulties in re-establishing marital relationships are compounded by the scarcity of men living in those areas. Ms. Ibrahimefendic also testified about the changing societal role of these women after the 1995 Srebrenica events. The victims that had undergone therapy showed significant improvement. However, Ms. Ibrahimefendic qualified that their condition oscillates and that regressions in their progress take place in some circumstances. Though optimistic, Ms. Ibrahimefendic anticipated that the children of Srebrenica would probably continue to face developmental problems. She testified that the road to recovery of these women and children who have received treatment is long. And in some cases, despite the therapy, recovery was not likely. She also noted that there were those women and children who did not receive any therapy at all and others who did not want any assistance. When asked by the Honourable Judge Rodrigues in the Krstic case, Ms. Ibrahimefendic was not able to say how many generations it would take for normal life to resume for these victims.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Ms. Ibrahimefendic, since your last testimony in 2000, could you briefly outline the work you have engaged in?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: During the past ten years, the Vive Zene organisation became a more professional organisation, which means that it started to work not only on individual wounds, not only with individual patients, women, but it also became active at the level of the community groups, families, and also on the education within the community, because there was a level of social destruction at the level of the community and the trauma. So there is a multidisciplinary team in Vive Zene that tried to create a special programme in order to work on recovery from trauma, not only at the level of the individual, but at the level of the entire community. In the meantime, I personally went through a lot of training, many conferences, meetings, conferences, and discussions with experts who deal with trauma. And in particular over the last decade or decade and a half, the world is beginning to look differently at traumatised persons because in the most recent wars a lot of civilians were casualties, so their suffering could not be marginalised. It could not be sidetracked. So at the international level, this matter became very important for the recovery of any community that had gone through war. I would just like to add that this means that science has made a lot of advancements in the treatment of trauma. New diagnoses have been developed. Not only has PTSD been linked with traumatised persons which as a consequence of war -- occurred as a consequence of war, but trauma has began to be looked at as a kind of process, as a process that is a continual one. This means that even though the war has stopped, the traumatic occurrence continues to develop within the people who are living in that society.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mrs. Ibrahimefendic, sorry, Ms. -- I realise that you have to tell us a lot about the development of this scientific area. On the other hand, Ms. Hasan has put to you a very specific question. And the Chamber would be happy if you could respond to that. Could you briefly outline the work you have engaged in since 2000; that was the question. And it would be helpful if you could focus on that, especially to save some time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Perhaps I can just restate the question a different way.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Have you continued to hold the position of co-ordinator of the Vive Zene programme since 2000?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I'm still the co-ordinator of the psychosocial programme. I continue to work with clients, I continue to work with families of missing persons. I am still working with women who were raped or persons who went through different kind of torture. I'm a member of the Vive Zene multidisciplinary team. And in the meantime, I have specialised in trauma; I'm trauma treatment specialist. In the meantime, I have also become an educator, a trainer, for other professionals in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I am also conducting trainings for victims and even professionals, investigators, researchers, policemen, people who are taking statements from victims who could be potential victims, because the OSCE, the organisation of the OSCE in Bosnia-Herzegovina, asked the organisation, and I'm the co-ordinator for that programme, to carry out trainings with prosecutors, investigators, and potential victims in order to motivate people to begin to testify. So I work not only at the level of the federation, I worked in Republika Srpska as well. I worked in the Bijeljina Prosecutor's Office, the Brcko district, together with victims, investigators, and my goal was to educate them about trauma so that they could know what a traumatic event or suffering has -- what sort of an effect has on people so that they could work with such people. So this is a brief summary of all the work that I have been carrying out over the past few years.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And during your work, have you treated women and children affected by the war from all over Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I worked with women, children, men who came from throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina who had experienced different traumatic events, because they lived in different parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And did you continue to treat the women -- the Bosnian Muslim women and children from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Women from Srebrenica were our clients as early as 1994, even before the fall of Srebrenica. We had a group of women that were staying as our inpatients while their husbands were in Srebrenica and I was a witness of all of their hopes that they would come back and that, as they said, Srebrenica would not fall. I was also working with them on crisis intervention, because they were afraid, they were in a panic at the time. And when the rest of their families were transferred to Tuzla, when members of their families were at the Tuzla Airport, members of our team were transporting them to the airport to meet up with their relatives. And then we monitored them throughout that whole period afterwards whether they had found their husbands, their fathers, their brothers, and so on and so forth. So we have been following up on these women and observing them throughout this whole process that they are going through.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I'd like to focus on these women and children of Srebrenica. And I'm going to ask you my question but I'll preface my question first by asking you: Do you recall testifying in the Krstic case about the suffering experienced by these women from the July 1995 events, and in particular I'm talking about the problems that made the suffering of these Srebrenica women and children different from the other trauma victims? Do you recall testifying on that issue in the Krstic case?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course I do remember that. Even today after 15 or 16 years the women still mention Potocari. They still talk about the times when they were being separated from their husbands. They talk about the time when they were detained in Potocari, about their departure to Tuzla, and so on. But in their daily lives as well, they are reminded of those times as well, because the graves are still being dug up, the process of identification is still going on. They are still under stress. The process of grieving has not started yet. They are still searching for their dear ones. The women in Tuzla on every 11th of the month go out and protest; they want to focus attention of the politicians and all of those others who have already for gotten about them to focus these people on themselves. They cannot forget their victims. So all those images from Potocari are still happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this Trial Chamber has heard evidence of the human remains that have been exhumed from the mass graves and that with the assistance of DNA analysis, some of these bodies and body parts have now been identified. Is it -- are you aware of this process of identification?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: The identification process is always a public one. Everything that happens is broadcast in the media, where mass graves are found, how many have been identified. So that I am updated about it, on the one hand. On the other hand, we participate in numerous conferences where missing persons are discussed, their suffering. Very frequently foreign organisations and domestic organisations organise meetings, conferences on that subject, results are summarised, how far we have come, what has been done. So these are all things that have to do with the exhumations and the process of identification. At such times perhaps our clients from 15 years ago ask us for assistance. They even ask us to provide an escort when they have to go for identification or when they have to ask -- when they are asked to recognise articles or items that have been found. They have the feeling that they cannot really bear it, so they do ask the social workers, the psychologists, and even doctors, for support, to go with them for support so that they would be able to face the bones, I would say, because then this is the final facing of the truth. So what struck me the most is that in a documentary film that was made, when a woman finds the bones of her son, she says, I believe in science but I don't believe my very own eyes, looking at the bones that were spread out on a piece of newspaper, paper. They were arranged on it. So these moments again cause upset and so in a way our whole team is there to provide support for these women whenever they need it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, based on your observations which come from your treatment of these women and children of Srebrenica, now that some of these women have had their -- the death of their relatives confirmed, have they been able to face that reality of death? Are their lives now back to normal?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: When you lose a loved one through normal losses, you go through a process of grieving. And this process of grieving has stages, from shock and disbelief that it happened, to the gradual acceptance of this loss. And after a certain period of time, you get back in your normal life and you start functioning normally again. However, when we're dealing with traumatic losses, then the process is a lot more complicated, primarily because they are missing people and you don't know what happened to them. So people will be burdened by the circumstances of their death, how they died, whether they were killed, whether they were executed, whether they had been tortured, hungry, thirsty, et cetera. So the grieving process can only start once you face and see the mortal remains that have been found. But whenever you -- whenever a person is identified and certain procedures are carried out and the family is informed that a person had been found and identified, then you establish the date for the funeral and then these people would go through the same process as if these people had just disappeared or just died. So they will go through the stages of disbelief, guilt, anger, all over again. On the one hand, they will accept these remains as belonging to that person and on the one hand they believe that this person is indeed dead, but there is still some hope left in them that this is not the truth. They accept these remains as something sacred and frightening at the same time. They are sacred because they had been told that the remains belonged to their loved ones, and at the same time this terrifies them because the knowledge means that there is no more hope, that there is nothing left to wait for and death is final. So on the one hand they can finally say, It's fine and there will be a place where I can bury them, I'll be able to visit the grave and I'll be able to go through the usual rituals that are organised after somebody dies in a regular way; and then after the remains are found, then certain rituals, religious rituals, are carried out. So in this way one could say that they face the death, and then the grieving process begins. And this process is very complicated. It's not simple at all. Many women have psychological twins to themselves, like they are unwilling to let go of that person. They dream about them, they talk to them. There are even certain objects that link them to the missing people or the dead people such as photographs or some objects that were a part of them. Even children can become what we call a linking object if there are children who had survived. So the grieving process is not the same as what it would be in case of a normal death, in case of a death that we all might face.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And in terms of the psychological impact, you previously testified about the symptoms these women and children were experiencing, including the nightmares, the irritability, the avoidance, depression, and so on; are these women and children -- are those symptoms still persisting in these women and children?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Well, the initial symptoms are those of reliving the event as if the event was happening at this very moment. People experience nightmares and then there are other intrusive symptoms that we discuss such as insomnia, anxiety, aggression, anger, and so on. After this many years, it can happen that even professionals or the women are able to connect their initial symptoms with the original traumatic event that happened 15 years ago. Now they are a lot more depressed and more isolated. They are bothered by crowds or company, they can't be in a group. There's a lot of distrust, primarily distrust towards one's own competency than distrust of others. They feel that others don't understand what had happened. They feel like they've been left to their own devices. On the one hand they feel isolated and feel empty. They feel like they can't experience love and can't experience joy and yet they can't experience grief either. Some of them are hypersensitive, one could say, and some are hyposensitive; so some are too sensitive and some not enough. Among those who are hypersensitive may have high blood pressure. There are a lot of psychosomatic problems, so they will frequently pay visits to doctors. And sometimes the doctors or the social workers might be a problem because they are not sensitive enough and they treat them as patients. And sometimes it's enough if they just ask them, Where are you from, what have you gone through? So a conversation, a simple conversation, might be a lot more effective than the bunch of medicines they are given. And I would just like to add that there are many of them who are apathetic, depressed; not sad, because sadness can be treated with medicine. Sadness is treated by sharing things, by meeting with people. There are lots of problems in the family, lots of problems with children, because some of these children have grown up, they are adolescents, and the culture is such that those who are not present are not discussed, they're not talked about. So there are a lot of children who have no information about their fathers. They don't know where their fathers went missing. Three days ago a woman came to see me - this was before I came to The Hague - and her 16-and-a-half-year-old daughter got married. She was ten months old when she arrived from Zepa with her mother and she had no photograph of her father or anything. And the mother, because of her own suffering, never had the energy to tell her about her father, to tell her about what he was like, or to tell her what she had heard about the circumstances of his death. So the girl went to Srebrenica to the registry, herself, and she asked the municipality to provide her with a photograph of her father and then she got very angry with her mother and left home. She told her mother, Everything is more important to you than I am. So there are a lot of problems with children now, because these children never process the loss rationally. They only listen to the stories of the adults. They were flooded emotionally, but depending on the age, they were not able to process this rationally or mentally.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't understand the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Ms. Ibrahimefendic, you have spoken a little bit about the breakdown of the relationships at the family level. I'd just like to ask you to tell us briefly about the relationships that exist at a community level based on your observations and interactions with these women and children. And if you can just talk about the period from 2000 until the present day, your knowledge from that period of time, because the evidence you gave in the Krstic case is evidence in this case, so we don't need to repeat that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you want me to tell you what's happening at the level of the society, what changes happened?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Correct. How are the July 1995 events experienced by these women and children affecting the relationships at the community level?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: The loss of such a large number of people in a day or two or three had a huge impact on the whole community, particularly because all these women arrived to Tuzla, they were accepted, and they survived. They made their decisions later to go to other towns or to other countries outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So not only were individuals destroyed, but all of society was destroyed, at the social, political, material, legal level. So society didn't have the capacity to handle all these problems, all the difficulties that happened, and society didn't provide adequate support and help at the time, the support that was needed in this sequence of traumas. And many families from Srebrenica, those who survived, started thinking about going abroad. A lot of my clients who were treated with us in 1995, 1996, and 1997 left Bosnia-Herzegovina and today live all over the world. Those who stayed decided not to return because what happened was -- was an extreme traumatic event. So returning to the place where all this happened was horrifying to them and it was traumatic. And the women, a lot of them, didn't dare return because they were afraid. Some did return. Some returned. But some continued living in Tuzla or elsewhere. However, there's a problem with their identity. They don't know who they are anymore, not even the children. Even though they might have lived in Tuzla for 15 years, when I asked them, Where are you from? The reply will be, I'm from Srebrenica. And that means that they haven't accepted where they are and they haven't integrated in the place where they are living. A part of their former identity is something they cannot forget and they continue to suffer because of Srebrenica, I think continue to think about what life was like before and how they lived before. The discussions among the surviving women whose husbands disappeared are very characteristic. In 2008 and 2009 until last year, I worked with a group of women whose husbands went missing, and among them were women who had one or more family member go missing. At the beginning, they all said things like, I found my husband, I found his head, I found his thigh bone, these weren't my husband's teeth, and so on. So the contents of the conversations that they have amongst themselves is still horrifying. And then you can imagine what goes on in the children's heads, what's happening to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And I'd like to now ask you about those children of Srebrenica. And, again, this is something that you discussed in your prior testimony, the impact of the children, so I'd like you to restrict your answer from your -- the observations you have coming from your treatment of these children post-2000. And I'd like to ask you: These surviving children of Srebrenica who, if I may say so, are the future of this group, can you tell us how the disappearance of the male population, be it their fathers, their brothers, uncles, cousins, the traditional providers in the patriarchal society that they live in, their leaders, and their role models, how does the absence of that part of their population affect their lives or -- affect their lives today?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: If during their development the children didn't have any models to identify with who would be the surviving men, or closer relatives, uncles, and so on, and if they didn't have the opportunity to share their experiences, the children will be rather lost and confused in all this chaos. Older adolescents act as if nothing happened, so the family members thought wrongly that they didn't feel anything. However, it was just too difficult for them to face this because in a way they were escaping from all of this. Younger children soaked in the older people's emotions, and when I talk to them individually and asked them whether they knew anything, whether they heard anything about their fathers, they would say things like, My family thinks I don't hear anything, that I'm asleep, but I can hear everything. I know that they found him, I know that they went to identify him, and so on. So there's this discussion with children. And children between the ages of five and ten can't understand the concept of death as being something final. Between the ages of five and nine, they think that death is a reversible thing and that those people who are now listed as dead will appear. There are children who have a lot of fantasy because as they have a lack of real information, real explanations, then in their imagination, they imagine their father, what he was like, what he looked like, and so on, and sometimes this can be very dangerous. And I have dealt with some cases and talked about this with some of my colleagues who work with children who say that children, in a lack of support and a lack of real information or because their mothers are being overprotective because they think that these children are incapable of handling such information, are in fact causing more damage. And as some of them grow, grow up, they are very concerned about their appearance. They think that they will be very strong. And when we ask them why they are taking so much care of their bodies and why they want to be so strong, they will mainly say that they don't know. But what's behind all this, in fact, is fear. They feel afraid, they feel threatened, even though there is no threat, there is no real threat. However, some things that they didn't experience also feel threatened.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And the impact that you have just described on the children, is that based on the -- your discussions with these children during the course of their treatment -- during the course of your treatment of them?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: It is based on conversations. What I'm saying now is based on my personal experience from my practice. I can give you an example. A mother brought in a young boy in 1997. He was five years old at the time. And last year she brought him in because he wasn't doing well at school, he couldn't focus, he couldn't study. He was always in his room, and he was always on the computer. He wasn't leaving the house or didn't have any friends. And when he came to therapy, I needed quite a lot of time to gain his trust so he would tell me anything at all about himself. It was very difficult, so I asked him to draw something for me. He is now in secondary school. And the drawing that he did was one that frightened me personally because it was the picture of a ghost and he said that this ghost was always present in his room, always standing in a corner, and that he sometimes talks to the ghost, and so on. However, when I tried to explain this to the mother, she denied all of this because on the outside he was very well developed, he was very handsome. And I would say that he's a psychiatric case. He needed the help of a psychiatrist. He was functioning at two levels. There was one part that he exhibited to the outside, that he exhibited to his friends. He talks to them to the degree that is necessary to him. He goes to school, he ignores the professors, doesn't talk to them much. And then he comes home in his inner world and then within himself there's this sense of terror that's constantly present. There's intense suffering, intense turmoil within him. And one could say that for him there are two realities: One, his inner reality that only he knows about, that only he is in contact with; and one that the others can't see. And in order to make peace between these two realities, one needs to handle these horrific images. One should share these horrific images with somebody, talk to somebody about them. However, from the very beginning, he is completely closed up and he is quiet. And another thing that's interesting, and the reason I mentioned him, is that he was a very hyperactive child when he first came to see us in 1997. He was very naughty. It was very difficult to calm him down. At the time, he was one of the most hyperactive children. And now he has turned into somebody who is completely closed up, who doesn't communicate anymore, and who is practically incapable of establishing contact with others. He is afraid of going outside. He is afraid of groups of people, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Ibrahimefendic, could you tell us if there's been any decrease or diminution of the impact on these women and children since you last testified in July of 2000?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Whether the impact of the war has diminished on women and children, well, that's a very complicated question because if we start from the theory that trauma develops not only as a result of the initial event but that it continues and that in this way it is reflected in various sequences, that is, it has its own shape in the various sequences, then it's very difficult to say whether the situation has improved. However, one can say that I'm personally very much engaged in seeing what helped these women survive, which psychological mechanisms gave them the strength to go through all of this, to continue with their lives, to assume the roles that were suddenly imposed upon them. And a lot of women have shown that in their recovery they have set goals for themselves and they relied upon these goals that they were supposed to achieve. They used various psychological mechanisms in order to protect themselves from the pain that they were experiencing. The initial denial and avoidance to think about the events that happened, even though these are negative mechanisms, they helped them continue their lives. However, parallel with the treatment of their individual wounds, it is very important to monitor the processes that are happening in society at the economic, social, and other levels, on the legal level, for example, to see how far the processing of war crimes has gone. So the process of the trauma continues but now it has a different shape. And capacities are being created for those who have developed these mechanisms to be able to continue handling the events that are currently happening. However, I would like to add that those who have still not found their relatives, it's as if time has stopped for them. And these families, together with their children, have a special traumatic process that they are going through. Their children are living the lives of their parents, namely, and in the lives of those families, there's only the past and the present. And the children are constantly in the situation that the mothers are helpless and they are those who are to provide their mothers strength to overcome this helplessness, but when there is an identification, for example, the past becomes the present and all the capacities for a future are destroyed. There is no longer any future. There is no vision of the future. It's very interesting when I ask, Can you imagine yourself where you will be in five years' time? And she would say, I don't know. They don't have any plans; they don't dare to plan, to make plans. They cannot imagine without fear, for example, that in five years my son will graduate from university. No. For them, this is something that is alien.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, I'm very sorry, I have to interrupt at this point in time. We must have our first break earlier than usual because I have a very urgent commitment in another Chamber. We must have our break now, and we will resume five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Ibrahimefendic, now Mr. Tolimir is conducting his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to greet Ms. Ibrahimefendic. I would like to wish her a pleasant stay amongst us. I wish for peace in this house. And I would like for the trial today, as well as the entire proceedings, to end as God wills and not as I will. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I have a few questions. First of all, I read your statement that you gave on the 20th of June, 2000, which doesn't contain as much data as you presented during this examination-in-chief. The other thing is, did the Prosecution ever ask you to write an expert report, and did you do that? Because that would be of more interest also to the Trial Chamber, to the accused, because then they would also have available the data that you are talking about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: No, nobody ever asked for my views. The trial never asked me or the organisation that I work for, for such a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we're going to cover today's questions during the examination-in-chief. On page 7, line 24, you said the children from Srebrenica, after they saw their father's being separated from their families, experienced trauma, they lost their identity. This is stated on page 8, line 4. So my question to you would be this: Do you know if they were separated in Potocari itself, the children from the families, or were they separated earlier from their parents when they decided that the families should go to Potocari and that they would go to attempt the break-through along the road that they took? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: The bulk of the children was separated from their fathers by saying good-bye from -- to them from home, at home. Some of them never got a chance to say good-bye to their fathers. A small number of them were separated in Potocari itself. I had a number of cases where the father and mother came together with the child to Potocari and they were separated from each other and the children saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since a younger population would tend to have younger children, let's say fighters, ranging in age from 20 to 30, they didn't avoid going to Potocari, they either did or didn't go there. Can you tell me whether this number is known to you and whether you investigated that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I don't know the number. We didn't research that particular aspect. Only on some occasions I heard from some women that, for example, the husband of one of them who was a teacher in school or was not in good health, they thought that if they went together with their wife that it would be better for them, but I don't know the number. We didn't investigate that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Ibrahimefendic. On page 10 of the transcript, lines 15 to 21 all the way to page 11, you talked about how you worked with women who were raped. Then after that, in line 21, you say: I am doing trainings for professionals who take statements from victims. I would like to ask you this in relation to this matter: Did you speak with any women who were raped in Srebrenica, or are you working with women who were raped in other places in society in the course of their lives?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I have five cases right now, five women from Srebrenica who are undergoing therapy and who were raped. They didn't speak about it up until 2000. They didn't talk about it when they came to therapy for the first time. But recently, now they are being sent to our centres by psychiatrists, their personality has changed quite substantially by now, some of them have psychiatric diagnoses, so they are being sent for treatment to our centre. Because we are a centre for therapy and rehabilitation and because we are a trauma centre, we are the only place in town where such persons can be accommodated, persons who had experiences of that nature. We have a lot of experience. We know a lot about trauma. So we are also engaged by others, for example, by courts, to train professionals so that they learn as much as possible about trauma so that in their contacts with victims they would be able to observe what is going on and to be able to create trust between them and the victims. For example, on the 19th of October of last year, I had 34 investigators in Banja Luka last year, and very young, very young policemen investigators who are processing war crimes, but they knew very little about trauma. And besides the trauma issue, they also had a problem in how to approach these people, and they expressed the desire of learning as much as possible in order to be able to approach a woman victim, a man who had been an inmate in a camp, they wanted to know as possible about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber, these five rape cases, do you know if these women were raped during the war in Srebrenica and do you have information about when this rape took place and how did this come about? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: These five women told us that they were raped in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you able to tell the Trial Chamber about one case? How did these rapes happen in such a short time when they were in the UNPROFOR base?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: They told us that they were going to get water, that the children were thirsty, that they went to get water behind the base building, that they were going towards the river, towards the creek, and that they were stopped there and that they were taken. They said -- for example, two women said that there were some tents where they were taken and raped. And there are even eye-witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Are you aware that the tents were something that only representatives of the UN had? Were their tents used for such activities? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. I don't know what the base looked like during the war. Later, I was in Potocari, I saw those buildings. I don't know how they were organised. I don't know if tents were there, how all of that was organised. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please provide any kind of documents that would talk about these matters for the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: No, I can't do that. But there is an Association of the Women Victims of War and that association has a database with all the women who were raped during the war, women who reported to that centre, who provided statements, stated all the circumstances, all the details of the rape. They brought witnesses. So this association can provide such data, not the organisation that I personally work for.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, are you able to tell us of any case of somebody agreeing to testify after the training and conversation with you, because you said you were training professionals who were taking victim statements? Thank you. And that after that therapy, victims were interviewed and they were brought before a court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Many victims are afraid. Even professionals are reluctant to come to court and to testify. On the one hand, they are afraid of how they are going to talk about what they experienced. This is one type of stress. The other type of stress is how to come before a Trial Chamber, how to come to court, and how to testify. Not because they're afraid. Not because they're afraid that they would be exposed to any kind of threat. It's more of their personal, individual fear before a Trial Chamber, being in court, because trials are quite stressful. I know that from personal experience. Regardless of the procedure that is followed in court, one has to approach the victims in order to have them come to testify. On the other hand, there -- they tell of their experiences during trials. For example, here they would talk about their experience, so the idea is for them to have as little stress as possible. But, actually, the whole story is not about preparing the witness about what they will say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Let me just add something: Well, the preparation consists of how to free the person of the fear, how to relieve them of the fear in order to be able to testify. How a victim can overcome obstacles in themselves in order to be able to come. The way in which they will talk about the traumatic experience is something that has an end, with the victim talking with the Prosecutor. So the way -- the preparation also consists of the way in which the victim will talk about their experiences.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Ibrahimefendic. I would like you to answer the specific part of my question in as many sentences as you see fit about things that I'm asking you about. The question is: Did the Prosecutor ever ask you to speak with any potential witness that refused to come because of that fear that you have just talked about? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: No, no. If you are thinking of this Prosecutor's Office, no. The Prosecutor's Office in Tuzla had problems relating to witnesses who refused to testify. And then we had these seminars, seminars that lasted for two or three days, where the victims would talk about the problems they encountered while testifying. The Prosecutor spoke about their problems in relation to this testimony, where they spoke to each other about problems that they had with each other. For example, there was a case where a witness told one of the Prosecutors in Tuzla, You spoke to me and while you were speaking to me you kept answering calls on your mobile phone. And she was very much bothered by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please not speak about events that are not related to Srebrenica. We have limited time.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: This is nothing to do with Srebrenica. This has to do with training, education, about trauma. Because in Bosnia the thinking is and the discussion is that it was necessary to explain to people that we are still in a certain trauma situation, going through certain trauma sequences, the trauma is still on-going, and that the trial proceedings have to go on. They have to be completed so that society can start moving in a different direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I would like to assist you. You have explained very well during the examination-in-chief the way you were educating professionals. Now, Mr. Tolimir is focusing on specific parts of your testimony. It's not necessary to go through these processes again. And the question was really a very clear one, and you said, No, I was not asked by this OTP, by this Prosecutor's Office. That was enough what Mr. Tolimir wanted to know. Please focus on the specific question. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mrs. Ibrahimefendic, on page 16, line 4, of today's transcript, you said that persons don't trust others, they are having a lot of problems, they cannot experience joy or love or grief. So what I'm interested in is: Did you speak with anybody who formed a new family after the Srebrenica event, and is that also true for them, that they cannot experience joy, love, and grief? Are there cases like that that you encountered?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course there are cases like this, but these relationships are always complicated. On the one hand they experience joy, on the other hand there is guilt because she is still alive, because she is sharing smiles with somebody else. So always in the background there is this sense of guilt for a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you very much. On page 17, line 9 to 21, you said: Three days ago this woman came to me with a 16-year-old daughter, and so on and so forth, and the mother never told her about her father and she went to Srebrenica and there she found her father's pictures and so on. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, can you answer my question, can you please tell me this: Would a child of six months, because you said that the child was six months old when she lost her father, can a six-month-old child have a feeling of intense loss of a parent, of a father, when they didn't even remember him or see him? Because you know a child of six months cannot remember anything. Or is this the case only with some people of that age who could remember and recall that?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: If a child doesn't have a father, they create one in their fantasy. All the children in the school that this girl attended, most of them, had fathers. She didn't have a father. So if she was denied information by her mother about her father's disappearance, if she kept telling her for five years, Your father is coming, your father is coming, he's alive, he's going to come back, and he never actually did come back, then the child lost her trust in her mother and stopped talking to her. The mother -- this is now the responsibility of the mother. And the treatment consists of strengthening the resources of the mother. A mother, and its her duty, she has to explain to the child what happened. She is the sole parent. She must try, because the child is not responsible for that, she must try to find a photograph or some kind of memento. But the child, in this case, had to do it herself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since the Trial Chamber is not aware of circumstances in Bosnia, how was a child able to go to Srebrenica on her own and how come they had a photo there and they didn't have anything at home, since nothing was left after the war in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: She found out in the registry office in Srebrenica, in the municipality where you would get your ID card, that the former documentation, the archive, before the war had been preserved and that her father had an identity card. So she went to the registry office where she asked for her father's file. She said, My father had an identity card before the war, so could you please look whether there is a photograph in that file. The woman and -- the girl said this, the woman very kindly found the file, gave her the -- gave it to her. So she photocopied the picture and she returned the document to the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Just a correction for the record: At page 17, line 13, the witness had testified that the child was ten months old and not six months old.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ten months old.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Ms. Ibrahimefendic, if you recall, on page 23 you said that many women try not to think about the problem and you said that this was a negative method. My question is: If that's a negative method, then in psychology, when they say that our lives are the same as our thoughts are, then is that a negative or a positive way? Does that mean that we shouldn't think about something negative in order to overcome it? Is there any contradiction there?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I said this in a different context, in relation to the psychological mechanisms of self-defence. If something is difficult for us, if we can't accept it, then we will deny it. And the mechanism of denial means that we're keeping ourselves in suspense, we're living a lie. However, this denial mechanism helped them survive. Imagine a situation where they were being transported to Tuzla and if at that point they had thought that their husband was dead, at that point they were denying that they were dead. They kept thinking that they were alive. So this mechanism helps them survive. Sometimes you can't accept the truth because it's very painful and we act as if it was not happening. We act as if it didn't happen. To this day, there are quite a lot of people, a lot of elderly women, who are trying to get their lives back from before the war. They picture that person alive. They dream about them, they talk with them. So this psychological twin exists. And in this way, they are denying reality. Others will say -- others will tell them, He's dead. And this person will say, No, to me he is not dead. So in that sense this psychological defence mechanism is not good for recovery. The question isn't how long it will take for them to accept the loss, the question is how they will face the truth. They have to ask themselves, How am I going to face the truth? I have a woman whose three sons are no longer alive and she says, How is that possible? And I can't answer that. So I'm trying to help her find a way to handle this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Ibrahimefendic. You talked quite a lot about the social situation that the families from Srebrenica found themselves in and you talked about the problem of losing a loved one. I would like to ask this: That social problem, is it experienced by all refugees, wherever they fled from in Bosnia, and do all those who lost a father in combat in the Tuzla region, at the front line, experience it the same way? Is it the same characteristics?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: That pain is universal. And everybody in Bosnia and Herzegovina or all over the world who loses a loved one, regardless of the circumstances, will experience pain. However, when it comes to missing persons, and there are a lot of them throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina, there is uncertainty and there is still some hope. There's a lot of ambivalence. On the one hand it's like they are alive, and on the other hand they're dead but there's no certificate. In normal circumstances, you need to know that somebody is alive or dead. But here, you're in suspense. And the pain is universal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Ibrahimefendic. Please tell us whether the social problems that we talked about, with all the refugees and everybody who went through certain trauma as a result of a loss of a loved one, and who moved into new communities, as there are a lot of people from rural areas who moved into towns, is this one of the reasons why they cannot return to their old places of residence? You can tell the Trial Chamber who's in power in Srebrenica, so they should be able to go back. But they don't want to go back because they are not used to that life, they don't know how to herd cattle. Did you consider this problem as well?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: When I think about this problem, I look at it from the psychological aspect. Namely, what once was will never return. And many people think that life should go on, that life should go on the way it was before the war. And when they return from where they had been expelled or from where they left, they realise that life is different. In the new communities, in the new towns, they had already started a life. The fact is that their children have grown up. So there's a problem within the family, because some want to go back and some don't want to go back. Some crave and long for their home and others don't long for their home. So conflicts regarding the return exist in the family. So that makes things complicated, as does unemployment, the economic situation, or the return to their original place of residence. And this means that they can't have medical insurance, they can't get educated. And social problems are similar in all of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you this because you're a psychotherapist, Ms. Ibrahimefendic, so are these problems complex because of all these aspects and because of this new situation -- so are these problems more expressed than during -- than the problems during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Well, of course the social aspect and the social dimension of traumatisation cannot be neglected. Apart from the psychological problems that I mentioned, such as things can't go back to the way they were, there are economic problems and there are political problems, legal problems, spiritual problems, and so on. And all these further complicated the situation, because society has been destroyed. A lot of mechanisms that kept society together and that provided a framework for the functioning of this society have been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Ibrahimefendic. I would be very interested to talk to you, but there isn't enough time. We are limited with time. In your statement, you said that from 1995 to 2000 you had about 60 women who you treated. My question is: Is there any sort of a database or a record of the people who you treated psychologically after the war, and could this be provided to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber can have all these documents. We have a very good database for each of our clients. For every visit they made there is a record of what we had discussed, the problems why they were admitted, how long they spent in our institution, how many times they came to therapy, whether it was outpatients treatment or not; these documents and the entire database is available, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Ibrahimefendic, for this conversation. I don't have any more time to ask you any more questions. I enjoy talking to you and learning something from you as an expert. We appreciate your expertise and I wish you a good journey, God bless you, and I wish you a good trip back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, thank you much. But you have more time if you need more time. You indicated one and a half hour and you have used little less than one hour. Just to make it clear: You have time if you want to continue. But it's up to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'm doing this because of the next witness. It was told that he has to be on today, and a lot of time was used up for the previous witness and this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Hasan, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I have no questions for re-examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Judge Mindua has a question for you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. I have a question for you. In today's record, on page 23, line 19 up to line 25, you explained very clearly that it's very difficult and very complicated to assess the consequences of the war, that is, what effect the war had on the lives of the women and the children and that it's very difficult to know whether and to what extent pain has diminished, whether the consequences have lessened. And on page 24, from lines 17 to 18, you said that the process of trauma continues but in a different way. I'm a little bit confused because I am translating the English transcript to myself in French. So, the cycle of trauma continues and it changes shape; that's what you said. So I would like to ask you the following question in relation to this: In these conditions, do pain, the suffering, and the trauma that caused it, are they incurrable? Is something like that incurrable? That is, is it possible at all to cure your patients, your clients; or should they be monitored, treated, all their lives? Is the therapy limited by time or not?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: What I said about the cycle of trauma and that the trauma continues, that the symptoms are there but in a different shape - I will say this very shortly - in relation to theory, that helps us strengthen our clients and our patients in this process of recovery. We go through the beginning of their trauma with them. Trauma goes through a cycle. First the expulsion, leaving home, getting to a certain destination where you're a refugee; then another shock when they become refugees. Although they think it's a safe place, they are worried and preoccupied with their physical survival, food, accommodation. And then in a way, they adjust; they develop some adaptive capabilities. They are still not aware of the psychological pain and trauma that they've been through. And since the war went on as long as it did in Bosnia-Herzegovina, some went abroad, then again it was a country where they didn't speak the language or it was a different language, then they adapted again, they developed new symptoms. They suffer because of the homes that they left behind. They adapt to the new circumstances, life goes on, their childrens [sic] grow up, they have new obligations, and they are exhausted. And then new trauma might occur such as Srebrenica in 1995, so they return home, and so on, and they find the dead. Each of these cycles has its own symptoms, traumatic events which are stressful for a particular person. And through this entire cycle of trauma, a person gets through by developing certain skills. And at the same time, their physical health and their mental health is weakened. Some people get through all these cycles successfully but they remain sad all their lives because practically trauma becomes a part of their life story. It's a part their personal history. And it determines their personal history and it determines their life. The traumatic event changes their life. Instead of everybody having a vision of how they will develop in life and what path they will take, something happens and it takes you in a completely different direction. And all of a sudden you have to leave your previous life behind. Even though you may want to forget it, you can't. You have to process it somehow. You have to take what's good in that life and then move into a new life. So some will continue to function, and they will exhibit normal functioning, but on the other hand there will always be something that they will regret, something that they will suffer for. I don't know if that's sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I see you are on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I am, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we release the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I was just going to address that very issue. And the reason why I'm on my feet obviously is because of General Tolimir's representation with respect to your question about whether he had any further questions. I just wanted to be clear on the record, because his response indicated that he was terminating his cross-examination in view of the witness that is following. I don't know what representations have been made to him with respect to the following witness. And in particular in light of the events that transpired yesterday, I want to be sure that General Tolimir is -- has completed his cross-examination appropriately, in other words, not based upon some representation or some understanding with respect to the following -- to the witness that will follow. And if that's the case, then I think it's not an issue, but I just want to be sure of that before we discharge this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. Mr. Tolimir, you heard the submission of Mr. Vanderpuye. What is your position on that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I thanked Ms. Ibrahimefendic and I gave her my blessing. Among us Christians, when you send a blessing, it's communication through God, so there is no returning to a previous point. I wished her a safe return home, so I don't intend to re-open my cross-examination. And I thank the Prosecutor for asking me to clear this up, but I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this common understanding. Ms. Ibrahimefendic, thank you very much that you came here to The Hague again after 11 years and for the help you could provide us. Thank you very much again, and now you are free to return to your normal activities. Good-bye. And the Court Usher will assist you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The next witness should be brought in. Dr. Brunborg will continue cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Please sit down. Welcome back, Dr. Brunborg, to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's good that you could make it again. And I have to remind you that the affirmation you made at the beginning of your testimony still applies. Mr. Tolimir has more questions for you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Brunborg. I would like you a pleasant stay [as interpreted], and I thank you for coming back. I apologise if you have had to come back again because of us. In any case, I would like to wish God's peace on you and all your activities. And I would like this cross-examination to end as God wills it and not as I will. I would just like to remind you of what we talked about last time, during your testimony on the 10th of February. We talked about the discrepancy between the B&H army data and the data of the International Committee for Missing Persons, which you used to draft your own analysis. The international committee had its own data negated by the B&H army, and we could see this on all the documents that were presented here during your testimony. What I would like to know is: Do you know if the Prosecutor's Office investigated the phenomenon of people who were killed earlier who were found in the graves? For example, if they were killed in 1992 or around that time but were found in a common grave in 1994? Thank you. Or 1995.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Information on this comes partly from the ICTY's own exhumations and investigations and partly from the ICMP exhumations. And as I said last week, I am not an expert on exhumations, but I believe if -- that there are certain mass graves were considered as Srebrenica-related, meaning that if a body was found in such a grave, it was accepted as a dead person, a person who died in connection with the fall of Srebrenica. There were a few cases, I've been told, of a mixture of deaths of people in 1992 and 1995, but these are only a few cases, perhaps only one, I've been told, about Bratunac. But I'm not an expert on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But we can see from your analysis that to a certain extent, just like in your answer now, you gave precedence to data of the International Committee of the Red Cross --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter would kindly ask the accused to repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the interpreter didn't catch your question. Please repeat it. I was asked by the interpreters. I stopped him to give him this information. Please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We could see on the list that we showed the last time that the army did not wish to accept, in a number of cases, that those persons were found in graves, even though the Red Cross claimed that their DNA was found in the graves. So my question is: These cases, and there were plenty of them - we cited ten of them here - do these cases deserve a special investigation so that we could see what this was -- what this was about? And why does it occur that different data is entered regarding persons in respect of the way that they died? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It may be an interpretation issue or a translation problem, but I think it would be helpful in either event with respect to this question if General Tolimir has a particular document in mind that he show it to the witness. The reason I raise it is because here we have a reference to the Red Cross claiming that DNA was found in the graves, and I think the record is quite clear that that's not what the Red Cross represented, and that is something that is more generally associated with the ICMP and -- the International Commission of Missing Persons. And so I think it would be helpful if General Tolimir has a particular document in mind, to show it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, it would help the witness to provide you with his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was thinking of the International Committee for Missing Persons, the ones that deal with the DNA, not the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And is it possible that the differences are so drastic that the B&H army did not accept them, in spite of the pressure that was exerted on them to do so? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you have a specific document in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I do have a document. This is 1776. Can we please look at it in e-court. Last time, we discussed it. So I thought that I wouldn't have to go over things again that we already had been over because of the time. This is the expert report of this witness, P1776.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And it would help the witness to refer to a certain page, for instance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think he refers to page 95 of our April 2009 report; is that correct? The English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your most important report, indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. If that would help the witness, then, of course, he can look at it. I was thinking of page 220; that was the last page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of the transcript? Page 220 of what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now, of your report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which has only 105 pages.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I didn't finish my sentence. I meant the 220 persons that are disputed in terms of data between the B&H army and the ICMP. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I'd like to sum up a little bit. More than 5.000 bodies have been exhumed and found dead, almost 5.500, by ICMP, and a few others have been identified in other ways. Matching with the army list, so that 70 per cent of those identified as dead were indeed also registered with the ABiH. When we checked the dates and place of disappearance, there were 220 out of these several thousand, 3-, or 4.000, exhumed bodies that had been reported as missing before -- not -- excuse me, not reported. Who were listed by the army as having died before 1995, that is, in 1992 or other dates, in spite of families having reported these as disappearing around the fall of Srebrenica. So first, it is less than 5 per cent that have inconsistent [Realtime translation read in error "consistent"] day of death. 220 out of 5.371. So it's a very small number, 3, 4 per cent.
